pentagon-raytheon-63-billion-sm3-ib-miss.content:
Raytheon has won a multi-year Pentagon contract worth up to $6.3 billion to build and sustain Standard Missile-3 Block IB interceptors, the Navy's principal defense against short- and intermediate-range ballistic missiles.

The Missile Defense Agency awarded the deal on Oct. 7, and Raytheon announced it the following day. Listed in the Pentagon's daily awards digest under contract number HQ0851-27-C-E001, it runs for five years with options for two more. The base value is $4.43 billion; if the options are exercised, the ceiling rises to about $6.34 billion.

The award is structured as an undefinitized contract action, a mechanism that lets work begin immediately while final terms are negotiated. The government obligated $454.2 million in fiscal 2026 procurement funds at signing — a fraction of the ceiling, and not the amount Raytheon will ultimately be paid. Work is centered on Raytheon's missile facilities in Tucson, Arizona, and Huntsville, Alabama, and is expected to run through Oct. 31, 2034.

## Replenishing combat-tested stocks

The contract's purpose is straightforward: rebuild the interceptor inventories the United States has spent in real fighting. The SM-3 was used in combat for the first time in 2024, fired by Navy destroyers defending Israel against Iranian ballistic missile barrages. Those engagements proved the weapon — and emptied magazines the Pentagon is now racing to refill.

"This award underscores Raytheon's commitment to increasing production of critical munitions," Raytheon President Phil Jasper said, describing the Block IB as combat-proven and central to keeping fleets and allies defended.

Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment Michael P. Duffey said the missile had "proven its operational superiority against any adversary," adding that the contract "provides production certainty to our defense industrial base, breaks sub-tier manufacturing bottlenecks, and ensures that our fleets and combatant commands have the interceptors required."

## What the missile does

The SM-3 Block IB is a midcourse interceptor. Launched from Aegis-equipped destroyers and cruisers — or from the Aegis Ashore sites in Europe — it climbs above the atmosphere, releases a kinetic kill vehicle, and destroys incoming ballistic missiles by sheer collision, carrying no explosive warhead of its own. The Block IB added an improved infrared seeker and better steering than earlier variants, sharpening its ability to pick real warheads out from decoys.

## Why multi-year matters

Demand for missile defense has climbed on nearly every front. Beyond the Middle East engagements, the war in Ukraine has shown what sustained missile and drone campaigns do to air-defense stocks, and U.S. planners are blunt that American magazines were sized for shorter wars. Multi-year contracts are the Pentagon's preferred answer: steady, predictable orders that let industry invest in tooling and suppliers with confidence rather than surging and stalling on single-year buys.

## A munitions buying spree

The award is the latest in a run of outsized Pentagon munitions deals. In October, Raytheon secured a contract worth up to $24.4 billion for Standard Missile-6 interceptors; in July, Lockheed Martin won a $58.6 billion Patriot missile contract. Together they reflect the administration's push to expand weapons production and lock contractors into long-term manufacturing commitments.

Raytheon says it has already been investing in expanded Standard Missile capacity. But industry executives have warned that congressional funding remains the binding constraint: without appropriated dollars, even signed contract ceilings cannot become production lines. For now, the SM-3 line in Tucson has its orders — and the Navy has one less magazine to ration.

boeing-wins-faxx-navy-stealth-fighter.content:
Boeing has won the Navy's F/A-XX contract, the award for the service's sixth-generation carrier fighter, in a decision announced Sept. 29 that hands the company both of the Pentagon's next-generation fighter programs.

The contract covers the full-scale development phase and is valued at more than $20 billion, including multiple test aircraft for ground, airworthiness, systems, and weapons integration testing. Boeing beat Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman. Northrop has requested a formal debriefing with Navy officials — the customary step before any protest.

## Why Boeing won

According to people familiar with the competition, Boeing prevailed on the strength of years of investment, decades of experience building carrier-based jets, and a design approach that matched the Pentagon's demand for fighters that are easier to upgrade across long service lives. The Pentagon required all three competitors to use common design standards so later modifications could be made quickly as technology evolves.

Boeing also leaned hard on digital design tools, letting engineers, military officials, and maintainers test changes virtually before committing to hardware — a pitch that resonated after the industry's recent struggles with cost overruns on fixed-price development programs.

"Now all of a sudden, it controls the next half century and beyond of US tactical aircraft," Richard Aboulafia of AeroDynamic Advisory said of Boeing. "There's nothing like that in history."

## Two sixth-generation programs, one builder

The F/A-XX award follows Boeing's March 2025 win of the Air Force's F-47, the manned fighter at the heart of Next Generation Air Dominance. With both programs, Boeing now holds the entire American sixth-generation fighter roadmap — a position Lockheed Martin held in the fifth generation with the F-22 and F-35.

"It's an honour to be selected to produce the Navy's first sixth-generation platform," Steve Parker, chief executive of Boeing Defense, Space & Security, said. "Delivering two advanced fighters in parallel was always our plan, and we invested accordingly."

The fighter will be built in St. Louis, Missouri, where construction continues on a secure manufacturing facility tied to an all-digital design and production system.

## What F/A-XX is for

The Navy describes F/A-XX as a sixth-generation strike fighter built around open mission systems architecture, advanced sensors, and greater operational reach — designed to fly farther, carry more, and operate alongside uncrewed collaborative combat aircraft. It is intended to begin augmenting, and ultimately replace, the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and EA-18G Growler, whose airframes are approaching structural and survivability limits against modern air defenses.

On the same day as the award, the Navy issued Boeing a contract to begin planning the shutdown of Super Hornet and Growler production — a signal of how the service intends to hand the St. Louis workforce and tooling from one generation to the next without a capability gap.

## The road ahead

Technical and programmatic details remain classified under national security rules. The program had at times looked vulnerable, with officials openly questioning whether the industrial base could handle two advanced fighters — plus Northrop Grumman's B-21 bomber — simultaneously. Awarding both fighters to one company may ease that strain through shared knowledge and economies of scale, though it concentrates enormous risk in a single contractor whose defense division has absorbed billions in losses on fixed-price programs.

First-flight timelines and production quantities have not been disclosed. The losing bidders' next moves — and the contract's finer print — should surface in the coming weeks.

taiwan-first-f16-block-70-arrive.content:
Taiwan's first two F-16 Block 70 fighters touched down at Chihhang Air Base on Oct. 2, ending a wait of nearly seven years and opening the long-delayed renewal of the island's fighter fleet.

The single-seat F-16Cs, serials 6727 and 6728, landed near Taitung on the island's southeast coast at about midday, escorted for the final stretch by Taiwanese F-16s and T-BE-5 Brave Eagle trainers flying in formation. They are the first of 66 Block 70 aircraft Taiwan ordered from the United States in 2019 under an approximately $8 billion deal known locally as the Peace Phoenix Soaring project.

## A long road from Greenville

The jets left Lockheed Martin's F-16 plant in Greenville, South Carolina, on Aug. 17, routing through Fort Worth, Hawaii, and Guam with support from a U.S. Air Force KC-135 tanker. They then sat in Hawaii for more than six weeks — held up first by weather, then by unspecified technical issues, and finally by a U.S.-imposed pause over the optics of a late-September meeting between President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

In a break with past practice, the aircraft had their U.S. Air Force markings removed before leaving Hawaii, revealing the Republic of China Air Force roundel underneath. On previous F-16 deliveries in the 1990s and 2000s, Taiwan's markings were kept covered until the jets arrived home, a nod to political sensitivities that this time was set aside.

The first Taiwanese Block 70 had been unveiled in Greenville in March 2025. Getting from rollout to delivery took another 18 months of testing and calibration to integrate Taiwan-specific systems, wiring, and software — on top of earlier supply-chain disruptions that had already pushed the program years behind its original schedule.

## Why it matters

Taiwan's fighter fleet is among the oldest in the region, and its pilots fly near-daily sorties shadowing Chinese military aircraft operating around the island. The tempo has worn airframes down, and the Block 70s bring relief: Northrop Grumman's AN/APG-83 active electronically scanned array radar, L3Harris's Viper Shield electronic warfare suite, conformal fuel tanks, and General Electric F110 engines put Taiwanese Vipers close to fifth-generation standards in sensing and networking, with compatibility for weapons including the AIM-120D, AGM-88, and Harpoon.

When all 66 arrive, Taiwan will operate more than 200 F-16Vs, counting the 139 older F-16A/Bs upgraded to a similar standard under a program completed in 2023. The new jets will equip the 7th Tactical Fighter Wing, stood up in December 2023, as Chihhang shifts from a training base to a frontline combat station.

## Beijing objects, Taipei presses on

China's Foreign Ministry restated its opposition to U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, with spokesman Guo Jiakun calling the position "consistent and clear." President Lai Ching-te, posting on social media, called the delivery an important milestone for air defense and said investments that raise the cost of any invasion help deter miscalculation.

Defense Minister Wellington Koo told lawmakers that additional jets would arrive before the end of the year, with more than 60 aircraft on the U.S. production line — some already at the delivery stage. After years in which the program became a test of whether approved arms sales could turn into real capability, the two Vipers on the ramp at Chihhang are the first tangible answer.

hacm-hypersonic-first-release-australia.content:
The U.S. Air Force has carried out the first flight-test release of its Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile over an Australian range, moving a long-delayed weapon into the air at last.

The War Zone first reported the test on Oct. 5. An Air Force spokesperson confirmed it the next day, saying the flight took place over "a designated Australian test range" and gathered "crucial data to advance the program's objectives." The spokesperson declined to give a date, describe the launch aircraft, or discuss speed and duration. Open-source reporting widely places the test at the Woomera range in South Australia's desert, the West's favored proving ground for hypersonic flight.

## A U.S.-Australian program

The test was conducted under the Southern Cross Integrated Flight Research Experiment, or SCIFiRE — a U.S.-Australian collaboration the spokesperson described as built on more than 15 years of partnership. Australia's vast, empty ranges offer the long flight corridors hypersonic weapons need, and Canberra is a full partner in the weapon: in Australian service it would be the country's first hypersonic missile and its fastest weapon, with planned carriage on the F/A-18F Super Hornet, EA-18G Growler, F-35A, and P-8A.

RTX's Raytheon is the prime contractor for the munition, with Northrop Grumman building the scramjet engine. The Air Force formally established the HACM program in 2022 after a 2020 industry solicitation. Its roots run deeper: the design draws on DARPA's Hypersonic Air-breathing Weapon Concept and, further back, the Boeing X-51 Waverider flights. The weapon has reportedly been designated AHM-4A under a new joint nomenclature series for missiles.

## How it works

HACM is an air-breathing hypersonic cruise missile. A conventional rocket booster accelerates it to high speed and altitude, then falls away; a scramjet engine takes over, sustaining flight above Mach 5 — more than 3,300 miles per hour — while the missile maneuvers inside the atmosphere. That combination, extreme speed plus the ability to change course in flight, is what makes hypersonic cruise missiles so difficult for air defenses built to track predictable ballistic arcs.

Unlike larger boost-glide weapons, HACM is sized to be carried by tactical fighters as well as bombers, which would let the Air Force hold defended targets at risk from many more platforms. Exact performance figures remain classified.

## Delays and the 2027 target

HACM has suffered significant delays — early plans aimed for flight testing years ago — and the Air Force has taken the unusual step of scaling back the overall test program to protect the schedule. The stated goal now is to be ready for a decision on rapid acquisition in 2027.

That urgency reflects the wider race: China and Russia have fielded hypersonic weapons while the United States has none in operational service. HACM is one of two hypersonic programs the Air Force is pursuing, alongside the larger AGM-183 air-launched rapid response weapon.

The spokesperson would say only that the recent test was "part of our continuous work to advance long-range strike capabilities." For a program that has lived mostly in renderings and budget documents, a real release over a real range is the milestone that counts.

anduril-navy-66-billion-submarine-indust.content:
Anduril Industries and the U.S. Navy have unveiled a $6.6 billion plan to expand America's submarine industrial base, anchored by a giant new manufacturing complex at Sparrows Point, Maryland.

The announcement came Oct. 6 at Tradepoint Atlantic, the former Bethlehem Steel site on Baltimore's waterfront, with President Donald Trump and Maryland Gov. Wes Moore on hand. Anduril will invest $3.7 billion of private capital to build Arsenal-2, a software-defined shipyard of more than two million square feet on a 187-acre site. The Navy has awarded the company a contract worth up to $2.9 billion, with payments tied to demonstrated production results rather than paid upfront — a structure the company says puts most of the execution risk on Anduril, not the taxpayer.

## Components, not whole submarines

Arsenal-2 will manufacture complex components and large assemblies for the Virginia-class attack submarine — items such as torpedo tubes and hull sections — and deliver them to General Dynamics Electric Boat and HII's Newport News Shipbuilding for final assembly. It will not build complete boats. The idea is to add a parallel source for the hardest-to-make parts, letting more construction proceed at once across the industrial base.

The planned facility includes high-bay assembly halls, fabrication areas, reconfigurable production lines, and a 1,200-foot graving dock, with road, rail, and waterfront connections for moving outsized assemblies. It will run on ArsenalOS, Anduril's manufacturing software, coordinating fabrication, assembly, material movement, inspections, and documentation. Permitting and site preparation are beginning now; initial operations are planned for 2030.

The project is expected to create 3,100 direct jobs and more than 11,000 indirect positions, generating about $2 billion in annual economic output.

## Why submarines can't wait

U.S. submarine production has been the Navy's pacing problem for years. The service wants to build two Virginia-class boats a year while simultaneously constructing the Columbia-class ballistic missile submarine — a workload the current base of two nuclear-certified yards and their suppliers has struggled to carry, with skilled labor scarce and lead times stretching.

On top of domestic demand sit the AUKUS commitments: Australia is to receive three, and possibly five, Virginia-class submarines starting in 2032. Meeting that pledge without shortchanging the U.S. fleet requires substantial growth in suppliers, infrastructure, and workforce — exactly the gap Arsenal-2 is meant to fill.

"Submarines are our oceans' apex predators," Vice Adm. Robert Gaucher, who oversees Navy submarine construction, said at the announcement — adding that they are needed "now more than ever" for deterrence, while acknowledging the country's shortfall in shipbuilding capacity.

## An unusual deal structure

In a surprise flourish, Trump said American taxpayers would receive a 40 percent stake in the new shipyard — held through a new Anduril subsidiary created to operate the facility, not as equity in Anduril itself. Further details were not immediately available.

"Today, we're officially launching the construction of the largest new shipyard in the United States," Trump said. "Since World War II, there's been nothing like what we're doing today."

For Anduril — a company built on drones, software, and autonomous systems — the move into heavy manufacturing is a leap. The bet is that tech-industry production methods can succeed where traditional shipbuilding has strained. If Arsenal-2 delivers, it could reshape how America builds undersea weapons. If it stumbles, the submarine programs counting on its parts will feel it first.

navy-orders-30-drone-ships-medium-usv.content:
The U.S. Navy has ordered 30 medium uncrewed surface vessels from three Louisiana shipbuilders, the service's biggest commitment yet to putting drone ships to sea in numbers.

The announcement came Sept. 29 under the Medium Unmanned Surface Vessel Family of Systems program. Galliano Marine Services, Huntington Ingalls Industries, and Saronic Technologies each received production agreements for 10 vessels, using Other Transaction Authority — a contracting route built for speed rather than the Pentagon's traditional years-long process.

## The money and the timeline

Each agreement covers 10 vessels at an average procurement cost of $40 million per hull, which works out to roughly $1.2 billion for the 30-ship run. Production begins immediately at yards in Loreauville, Houma, and Franklin, Louisiana, with the first deliveries due before the end of fiscal year 2027.

Seven companies competed after completing Phase I at-sea testing. The losers — Sea Machines, Leidos, PacMar Technologies, and Birdon — did not get production deals, though three of them received $15 million each for completing the trials and will be listed on the Defense Department's drone marketplace, keeping them eligible for future work.

## What the Navy asked for

The MUSV marketplace solicitation, issued in March to replace the earlier Modular Attack Surface Craft effort, called for vessels able to cover 2,500 nautical miles at 25 knots while carrying 25 tons on the payload deck. In Phase I, the Navy tested whether the contenders could sense their maritime surroundings, sail without operator assistance, and stay deployed for extended periods.

Saronic will build its 180-foot Marauder design; HII offered Romulus. Galliano Marine Services, which does business as Edison Chouest, has not publicly detailed its entrant.

"Each agreement is for the procurement of 10 MUSV at an average procurement cost of $40 million per vessel," Chris Miller, the Navy's acting portfolio manager for robotic and autonomous systems, told reporters. He called the awards "a significant step forward in translating the strategic vision into a tangible fleet capability."

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao framed the move as the service's priority to modernize the fleet quickly with autonomous systems.

## Why "medium" matters

Medium USVs sit in the sweet spot the Navy has chased for a decade: big enough to carry meaningful sensors and weapons across ocean distances, small and cheap enough to buy in numbers and risk in contested waters. They are central to the "hybrid fleet" vision — a relatively small number of large manned warships multiplied by scores of robotic ones doing surveillance, mine warfare, electronic warfare, and strike.

Past efforts foundered on reliability, autonomy shortfalls, and shifting requirements. The Navy's plan now is to grow the uncrewed surface fleet from four hulls to 30 by 2030, focused on the Indo-Pacific. Whether these 30 boats become an operational capability or another experiment with hull numbers will depend on what the at-sea testing actually proved — results the Navy has not published in detail.

The choice of Other Transaction Authority is itself a statement of intent. OTA agreements let the Pentagon prototype and buy without the years-long Federal Acquisition Regulation process, and the Navy has used them deliberately here to compress the timeline from competition to hulls in the water. The losing bidders' exclusion from standard protest rights under OTA is part of that trade-off: speed in exchange for the usual legal recourse, a bargain the Navy has decided is worth making as it races to field uncrewed mass in the Pacific.

sweden-first-patriot-mission-poland.content:
Sweden will deploy a Patriot air defense unit to Poland in December, the first time Stockholm has sent the U.S.-made missile system on a NATO mission.

The government announced the decision Oct. 6. About 100 personnel from the Air Defence Regiment, supported by the Blekinge Air Wing, will operate the system — known in Swedish service as Luftvärnssystem 103 — under NATO command as part of the alliance's Integrated Air and Missile Defence.

## Guarding the Ukraine lifeline

The unit's task is to protect the NATO logistics hub at Rzeszów in southeastern Poland, the key node through which Western military and civilian aid flows into Ukraine under NATO Security Assistance and Training for Ukraine. The vast majority of military donations for Ukraine transit through Poland, and NATO has reported the hub handling on the order of 18,000 tonnes of materiel a month.

In an era of long-range precision weapons, a rear-area logistics hub is a frontline target. Sweden's deployment puts a scarce, high-end defensive asset over the infrastructure that keeps Ukraine supplied — and over NATO's own ability to move forces across the eastern flank.

"As Allies, we share responsibility for protecting and defending NATO territory," said the Chief of the Swedish Army, Johan Pekkari. "By deploying advanced capabilities from the Air Defence Regiment and Blekinge Air Wing, Sweden will strengthen NATO's eastern flank in Poland while helping to protect the vital support effort for Ukraine."

"The security environment and the complexity of the mission place significant demands on the unit," said Sofia Westermark, commander of the Air Defence Regiment. "We are well trained, well prepared and have the right composition to accomplish the mission."

## Timeline and politics

The mission is set to run from early December through the end of 2026, with preparations underway for a possible extension into the first half of 2027 — an extension that would require the Riksdag's consent, Defense Minister Pål Jonson has noted.

Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said the deployment safeguards the flow of support to Ukraine while strengthening the alliance's eastern flank. It follows a separate Swedish contribution announced days earlier: Gripen fighters began flying NATO missions over Poland on Oct. 1, supporting air defense over the same logistics corridor.

The deployment lands in a charged domestic moment. Sweden joined NATO only recently, and the question of how far Swedish forces should deploy in collective defense remains contested in Stockholm — making the decision to send one of the country's most capable air defense systems abroad as much a political statement as a military one.

Patriot, built by Raytheon, is the alliance's standard for intercepting ballistic and cruise missiles and aircraft. For Poland, already hosting a growing web of allied air defenses, the Swedish battery adds another layer. For Sweden, it marks the step from new ally to burden-sharing contributor — putting hardware, not just signatures, behind its NATO commitments.

The deployment also underscores how seriously NATO now takes the air threat to its rear areas. Russian long-range strikes have repeatedly targeted Ukrainian logistics, and allied air defenses in Poland have been kept on high alert as Russian aircraft and missiles operate near the alliance's borders. Positioning a Patriot battery over Rzeszow is a recognition that in a modern missile war, there is no safe rear — only defended ones.

pentagon-lockheed-f35-multiyear-deal.content:
The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin are discussing a sweeping multi-year agreement for the F-35 that could span up to a decade and cover both building the jets and keeping them flying — a deal potentially worth tens of billions of dollars.

The talks were first reported by Breaking Defense on Oct. 9. The idea is not new: officials have weighed multi-year F-35 procurement for years. But the current push, driven by the administration's enthusiasm for long-term weapons agreements, would go further than past efforts by bundling production with sustainment — the maintenance, spares, and support that have long been the program's costliest headache.

## What a decade-long deal would include

"There's been talk about a 10-year, multi-year buy that would include the production as well as sustainment," Matt Milas, president of Honeywell Aerospace's defense division, told Breaking Defense in September. Honeywell is a major F-35 supplier.

A central element would be bulk purchases of spare parts, with the increased flow of components expected to begin around the jet's 21st production lot, roughly three years out. Flooding the supply chain with spares is seen as the most direct lever for lifting the fleet's readiness rates, which have long trailed the Pentagon's targets.

## The skeptics

Not everyone is convinced the structure fits. A person familiar with the negotiations, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed the talks but questioned their premise: multi-year procurement "makes sense where the department has seen success with munitions contracts. It makes less sense for aircraft lot buys" — particularly while elements of F-35 modernization are still in development. "The complexities of sustainment present multiple unique challenges," the person added, doubting Lockheed could demonstrate genuine long-term savings.

The skepticism has history behind it. The F-35's sustainment bill — the cost of operating and maintaining the fleet over its lifetime — has been the program's most stubborn problem for a decade, with per-flight-hour costs resisting years of reduction campaigns. With more than 1,000 jets delivered worldwide, even small shifts in sustainment costs move tens of billions of dollars.

## The backdrop

The talks come days after the Pentagon finalized its deal for F-35 Lots 18 and 19: 296 aircraft for $24.3 billion, an average of $82.4 million per airframe, with deliveries starting this year. Lot 20 is expected to be negotiated as a multi-year contract now that the program is in full-rate production, and Lockheed chief executive Jim Taiclet has said the company can sustain production at 156 jets a year on the strength of U.S. and allied demand.

The Pentagon also continues to spend heavily on the support tail: a recent $1.6 billion spare-parts award was described as the largest in the program's history, and the Navy added $871 million to Lockheed's site-activation contract for standing up new F-35 operating locations.

No timeline for an agreement has been announced. Whether the two sides can bridge the gap between the Pentagon's appetite for long-term savings and industry's caution about locking in sustainment costs will determine whether the decade-long deal becomes the template for the fighter's future — or another idea that stalls in negotiation.

gdls-perch-2-loitering-munitions-army.content:
General Dynamics Land Systems will deliver four prototypes of its PERCH 2.0 loitering munition system to the Army by the end of October, putting a new tank-launched drone capability into soldiers' hands within weeks.

The prototypes are headed to the 1st Brigade, 1st Cavalry Division at Fort Hood, where troops will integrate them onto Abrams tanks for experimentation, Scott Taylor, GDLS's director of U.S. growth, told Breaking Defense. The upgraded system is set for its formal debut at the AUSA exposition in Washington this month.

## What PERCH is

PERCH — Precision Effects & Reconnaissance, Canister-Housed — is a modular kit that bolts onto M1A2 Abrams SEPv3 tanks and Stryker vehicles and lets crews launch AeroVironment Switchblade 300 loitering munitions without opening their hatches. The munitions serve as both scouts and strike weapons: loitering over the battlefield to find targets beyond the line of sight, then diving onto them.

The 2.0 iteration reflects direct Army feedback on the first version, which GDLS debuted at last year's AUSA. Soldiers asked for better beyond-line-of-sight capability, easier reloads, and more onboard storage — addressed in part by switching from the larger Switchblade 600 to the smaller Switchblade 300 — plus the ability to fire while fully buttoned up, preserving the vehicle's armor and chemical-biological protection.

The system was refined after a December 2025 demonstration at the Machine Assisted Rugged Sapper event at Fort Hood, where the launcher was tested on Abrams tanks in realistic mission scenarios.

## Built for Ukraine's lessons

GDLS developed the original PERCH with its own research funding, Taylor said, in direct response to the war in Ukraine, feedback from U.S. commanders in Europe, and discussions with III Armored Corps leadership. Loitering munitions have become one of the war's defining weapons, used by the thousands against armor, artillery, and air defenses.

The goal is to give armored brigades their own organic drone-strike capability — the ability to see and hit targets beyond ridgelines and buildings — rather than waiting on assets controlled at higher echelons. In GDLS's concept, the tank becomes a node in a sensor-to-shooter network, launching expendable eyes that can turn into precision weapons when a target appears.

## An urgent Army market

The Army has been moving quickly to push one-way attack drones down to brigade level and below, and several companies are competing for a role. GDLS's advantage is incumbency: it builds the Abrams and the Stryker, and PERCH is designed as a bolt-on kit requiring no permanent changes to the vehicle — a replacement of the turret's rear sponson box and mounting on existing hardpoints.

The company has not disclosed the system's range, warhead details, or expected unit cost. What happens at Fort Hood over the coming months — how soldiers actually use the prototypes, what breaks, what gets requested — will shape whether PERCH 2.0 moves from experiment to a program of record. For now, the prototypes are built, the brigade is waiting, and the clock is ticking toward the end-of-October delivery.

The munition at the heart of the system, AeroVironment's Switchblade 300, is a tube-launched loitering weapon already in U.S. service, small enough to be carried in numbers and precise enough for targets that do not justify larger fires. Pairing it with armor gives tank crews something they have never organically had: their own aerial reconnaissance that can become a strike asset in seconds, without calling up the chain of command.

australia-second-himars-tranche-early.content:
Australia has taken delivery of a second tranche of U.S.-built HIMARS rocket launchers — two years ahead of schedule and just a year after the first.

The announcement came Oct. 7 from the Defence Minister. The launchers go to the Army's long-range fires regiment in Adelaide, part of the 10th Fires Brigade, significantly expanding a capability Canberra considers central to its military reorientation toward the Indo-Pacific.

## Ahead of schedule, twice over

Early delivery has become something of a theme for Australia's strike programs. The country fired a Precision Strike Missile from a HIMARS during Exercise Talisman Sabre 2025 — two years ahead of schedule — and earlier this year successfully test-fired the first Australian-manufactured Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System missile from one of its own launchers.

"These highly mobile systems are an incredibly important platform and the delivery of these additional units represents a significant leap in capability for the Australian Army," Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said.

## The 90-launcher plan

The second tranche feeds a much larger ambition. In April, the government announced additional investment in HIMARS and Precision Strike Missiles to stand up a second long-range fires regiment. At full strength, Australia plans to operate up to 90 HIMARS across two regiments within the 10th Fires Brigade.

The ranges are growing too. PrSM gives the force the ability to strike targets up to 500 kilometers away; future increments are expected to push beyond 1,000 kilometers — a reach that would let land-based launchers hold distant maritime and land targets at risk across Australia's northern approaches.

## Building missiles at home

Canberra is pairing the imported launchers with a sovereign munitions effort. Australia and the United States established a cooperative PrSM program last year, and missile production is already underway at a new facility in South Australia, with a second factory due to open near Newcastle, New South Wales, next year.

The investments sit inside the 2026 National Defence Strategy and Integrated Investment Program: up to $37 billion for long-range strike capabilities, and up to $36 billion over the decade for the Guided Weapons and Explosive Ordnance Enterprise.

## Why HIMARS

The truck-mounted system earned its reputation in Ukraine, where precision rockets destroyed Russian ammunition depots and command posts far behind the front lines. For Australia, the appeal is the same: mobile, hard-to-find launchers able to deliver precise long-range fires — and, increasingly, Australian-made rockets to feed them.

The first Australian HIMARS were displayed publicly at the Avalon airshow in 2025. With the second tranche now in country two years early, the program has become a rare bright spot in a procurement landscape more often defined by delay — and a signal of the priority Washington places on arming allies in the region.

The program's pace stands out against its own original plan. The first tranche began with two launchers shown publicly at the Avalon airshow in 2025, and the delivery schedule at the time called for six more by mid-April, another 12 during 2026, and the remaining 22 before the end of 2028. The second tranche arriving two years early suggests both production and the U.S.-Australian coordination behind it are running well ahead of expectations.
